topic.title: the equal-bill friendship
topic.claim: The first time you earn more than a close friend, you start ordering cheaper when you eat with them.
topic.moment: dinner with a best friend after the salaries split

cover.headline: Earn more than your best friend, and you [start ordering cheaper].
cover.sub: Nobody told you to. You just did.

paragraphs: Earn more than your best friend, and you start ordering cheaper.
Same college. Same canteen. Same broke last week of every month.
Then the offer letters came. Yours was double theirs.
Now you're the one scanning the menu for the cheap side first. You say "I'm not that hungry." You pick the place near their office, not yours.
When the bill comes, you split it exactly. Never more, even though you could.
Because paying for both of you would say the thing out loud.
Friendships here run on being equals. The moment one of you is visibly doing better, everything gets managed so the other one doesn't feel it. Call it the equal-bill friendship.
And your friend knows. They notice you ordered the dal when you could have had anything.
And I don't think it's pity.
It's the most Indian kind of love: protecting someone's pride by pretending there's nothing to protect.
**You can afford the expensive dinner. What you can't afford is your friend noticing.**

end.send: Send to the friend you always split the bill with, exactly.
end.save: Read it before your next dinner with them.

claims.text: When one friend starts earning significantly more than the other, the higher earner unconsciously spends less around the friend (ordering cheaper, matching the other's budget) because the friendship depends on perceived equality and any visible status gap gets managed away to protect the other's pride.
claims.sentence: Earn more than your best friend, and you start ordering cheaper. ... Friendships here run on being equals. The moment one of you is visibly doing better, everything gets managed so the other one doesn't feel it.

80c214a029f049f0d08b6d48803904b05a5a937c.broken_premise: None. Every load-bearing claim in this post is an interpretation of motive and a generalization about everyday behavior (the higher earner orders cheaper, under-spends, splits exactly, to protect the friend's pride). The one concrete, checkable action — 'split it exactly' — describes a choice, not a fee, tax, price, contract or market rule. There is no mechanism of law, pricing, or who-pays-for-what that the post misstates, so there is nothing to falsify.
80c214a029f049f0d08b6d48803904b05a5a937c.actual_mechanism: The post isn't an empirical claim about a system; it's a reading of a social dynamic. The underlying behavioral logic is well-documented: people manage relationships through social comparison and seek to avoid status threats that destabilize equal-status friendships, and conspicuous generosity can read as status assertion rather than kindness — so down-playing one's advantage is a recognized face-saving move. The post interprets this as love/pride-protection, which is an opinion about motive and not a testable financial fact.
